why-ai-pilots-stall.quote: The useful denominator is an accepted business outcome.
lab: Find the cost hiding in the workflow
Meridian is comparing a drafting assistant with its current service process. Change the assumptions to see what AI processing and human review contribute.
questions: What is the unit of value, and what is its current baseline?
How much review and exception work remains per task?
What evidence earns the next stage of investment?
Who can pause the system and own the fallback?

shadow-ai-biggest-exposure.quote: Govern the route people actually use.
lab: Same task. Different exposure.
A Meridian analyst wants to summarize a supplier proposal. Explore how the account and integration change the questions to ask.

steps.label: Personal account
steps.title: Which agreement covers this upload?
steps.text: The familiar product name does not establish an approved data path. Check the actual account, terms, retention, and the sensitivity of the proposal before uploading it.
steps.evidence: Approved account and permitted data classification

steps.label: Managed workspace
steps.title: What does the managed route permit?
steps.text: A managed workspace can provide organizational controls, but access still needs a defined purpose. Confirm who can share outputs or add connectors and how requests are logged.
steps.evidence: Workspace settings and sharing review

steps.label: Connected workflow
steps.title: What can the integration retrieve?
steps.text: A connector expands the reachable data. Test the real user permissions and remove sources the task does not require. A sanctioned tool can still expose overshared material.
steps.evidence: Connector scope and representative permission tests

questions: Which account and agreement govern each workflow?
What data may people submit or retrieve?
Is the approved path fast enough for the real task?
Who handles a suspected disclosure or unapproved integration?

you-dont-control-the-control-plane.quote: An exit plan is an operating option you have tested.
lab: Which dependency deserves a plan?
Meridian is reviewing a critical AI service. Explore the questions behind four provider-controlled conditions.

steps.label: Lifecycle
steps.title: A version is scheduled to retire
steps.text: Trace the notice to the workflows that use that version. Assign a migration owner and a date for representative testing.
steps.evidence: Dependency inventory and migration window

steps.label: Capacity
steps.title: Peak demand exceeds the allocation
steps.text: Confirm the actual deployment limits and queue behavior. Decide which work can wait, degrade, or move to another route.
steps.evidence: Load test and service terms

steps.label: Data conditions
steps.title: A feature stores application state
steps.text: Review the feature’s actual retention and deletion behavior, including any contractual exceptions.
steps.evidence: Feature-level data-flow record

steps.label: Exit
steps.title: A preferred alternative is available
steps.text: Test the alternative on your evaluation set and estimate the changes to prompts, integrations, and staff workflow.
steps.evidence: Migration rehearsal and accepted tradeoffs

questions: Which provider changes could interrupt a material workflow?
Which fallback has been tested with real work?
What do our actual capacity and data terms commit to?
Who owns the lifecycle calendar and exit rehearsal?

the-90-day-platform-stand-up.quote: The first quarter should produce a service, a decision record, and a cadence.
lab: Build the mandate into the work
Explore Meridian’s illustrative first-quarter plan. Each phase has an accountable role and a concrete output to review.

steps.label: Days 1–30
steps.title: Make the approved path usable
steps.text: Agree decision rights and deliver one sanctioned workflow with clear data conditions, an owner, and a support route.
steps.evidence: Signed mandate, initial register, and a working access route

steps.label: Days 31–60
steps.title: Make the operation observable
steps.text: Connect usage, cost, quality checks, exceptions, and provider dependencies to the business workflow.
steps.evidence: Operating dashboard and intake decision records

steps.label: Days 61–90
steps.title: Prove that decisions can be made
steps.text: Exercise a realistic disruption and review the portfolio against agreed evidence. Record what expands, changes, or stops.
steps.evidence: Failure rehearsal, portfolio decisions, and next-quarter backlog

questions: Who can approve, pause, or stop a deployment?
Which useful approved route will we ship first?
Can we connect cost and quality evidence to a business owner?
What disruption will we rehearse before the quarter ends?

excessive-agency-ai-risk-no-attacker.quote: Every permission is a decision about what a mistake may change.
lab: What did we actually authorize?
Meridian needs an assistant that reads an approved email queue and prepares summaries. Toggle optional permissions to see how its reachable actions expand.
questions: Which individual actions does the task require?
Are resource permissions enforced by the receiving service?
What exactly does a human see before approving an action?
Can we pause the workflow and identify what changed?

ai-supply-chain-attack-surface.quote: Trust the reviewed component and configuration—not the label on the ecosystem.
lab: Follow the trust boundary
Explore a fictional Meridian supplier-analysis workflow. Each layer asks a different question of the owner approving it.

steps.label: Artifact
steps.title: What is being loaded?
steps.text: Verify origin, version, digest, serialization format, and whether loading invokes custom code.
steps.evidence: Artifact record and approved loading procedure

steps.label: Runtime
steps.title: Where does the code execute?
steps.text: Constrain credentials, filesystem access, network reach, and dependencies to the task.
steps.evidence: Runtime configuration and dependency inventory

steps.label: Tool connection
steps.title: What authority crosses the interface?
steps.text: Review the server implementation, identity, allowed resources, and tool operations.
steps.evidence: Scoped authorization and reviewed server version

steps.label: Update
steps.title: What changes after approval?
steps.text: Track notices and revisions. Re-evaluate changes that alter execution or authority, and keep a revocation path.
steps.evidence: Change record and recovery rehearsal

questions: Can we identify the exact artifacts and versions in production?
Does loading or connecting execute code we have reviewed?
What credentials and resources can each component reach?
Can we revoke or replace a component without losing the incident trail?

model-deprecation-reliability-risk.quote: A successful API call is not a successful migration.
lab: Rehearse the migration before the deadline
Meridian has received a retirement notice for a model used in customer service. Walk through the decisions that connect the notice to a safe operating change.

steps.label: Discover
steps.title: Which workflows depend on this version?
steps.text: Confirm the precise deployment and date, including update behavior. Identify every affected business owner.
steps.evidence: Verified dependency list and current provider notice

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.title: Does the replacement satisfy the task?
steps.text: Compare representative cases, critical failures, cost, latency, and reviewer effort. Review differences with the accountable business owner.
steps.evidence: Accepted evaluation and explicit tradeoffs

steps.label: Release
steps.title: What evidence would stop the cutover?
steps.text: Choose a bounded release, monitoring, escalation, and a person authorized to pause it.
steps.evidence: Release plan and stop conditions

steps.label: Fallback
steps.title: What remains available after retirement?
steps.text: Rehearse a route that does not depend on the retired version. State its capacity and limitations.
steps.evidence: Usable fallback and recovery record

questions: Which deployed versions and update policies do we depend on?
Who accepts behavioral changes after evaluation?
What live signal pauses the release?
Does the fallback still exist after the retirement date?

five-things-vendor-pitch-leaves-out.quote: Buy the operating conditions, not just the demonstration.
lab: Bring a better question to procurement
Explore the evidence Meridian should request before approving a new enterprise AI agreement. These are diligence prompts, not claims about every vendor.

steps.label: Unit economics
steps.title: Show the cost of an accepted result
steps.text: Use a representative workload and include corrections, review, and supporting services.
steps.evidence: Task-level cost and quality comparison

steps.label: Capacity
steps.title: Show the actual service commitment
steps.text: Separate price arrangements from quota, availability, and recovery behavior.
steps.evidence: Applicable terms and a peak-demand plan

steps.label: Data
steps.title: Show the feature-level data path
steps.text: Trace retention, application state, access, deletion, and downstream integrations.
steps.evidence: Configured data-flow record

steps.label: Controls
steps.title: Show the governed configuration working
steps.text: Test useful task completion and misuse handling with the intended controls enabled.
steps.evidence: Representative governed evaluation

steps.label: Readiness
steps.title: Show what must change inside our organization
steps.text: Identify access and content issues that could affect deployment, with an owner for each.
steps.evidence: Prioritized remediation and ownership

questions: Can we compare cost per accepted task using our workload?
Which contractual terms govern demand and interruption?
Have we checked the data behavior of every required feature?
Have we evaluated the intended controls and permissions?
Who owns the information cleanup and ongoing access review?

ai-act-obligations-already-binding-you.quote: One AI program can contain several legal roles and several deadlines.
lab: Which clock are you looking at?
Select an obligation track. This is a dated overview, not an applicability test; scope, exceptions, and transitional conditions require a system-specific review.

steps.label: Early duties
steps.title: Start with literacy and prohibited practices
steps.text: The Commission dates these provisions to February 2, 2025. Check which activities and personnel are in scope for your systems.
steps.evidence: Role-specific review and documented operating measures

steps.label: Transparency
steps.title: Review the Article 50 track
steps.text: The main application date is August 2, 2026. Distinguish provider marking, interaction notices, and applicable deployer disclosure duties. See the linked FAQ for the narrow legacy-system marking transition.
steps.evidence: Applicable duty mapped to the released experience

steps.label: High risk
steps.title: Classify before planning conformity work
steps.text: Commission guidance gives December 2, 2027 for Annex III uses and August 2, 2028 for relevant product-embedded systems. Review the exact system and transition conditions.
steps.evidence: Classification rationale and implementation plan

steps.label: Change review
steps.title: Keep the determination current
steps.text: A new purpose, user population, feature, or deployment arrangement can require another review. Assign a trigger and a named decision owner.
steps.evidence: Dated review record and unresolved questions

questions: Have we recorded purpose, geography, and legal role for each system?
Which duties and transitions actually apply to that use?
Where are relevant notices and controls visible in the workflow?
Who reviews a change in purpose, feature, or applicable law?

sources.title: European Commission: navigating the AI Act

who-owns-the-ai-decision.quote: A mandate becomes useful when people know which decisions they can make.
lab: Follow the decision through the organization.
Meridian wants to release a customer-service assistant. Choose a role to see its authority, its boundary, and the evidence it brings.

steps.label: Business
steps.title: Define what an acceptable outcome looks like.
steps.text: The service owner sets acceptance criteria, assigns reviewers, and owns customer outcomes. A promising demo does not grant authority to expand data access.
steps.evidence: Baseline performance, reviewed examples, exception handling, and named operating capacity.

steps.label: AI function
steps.title: Provide a dependable approved route.
steps.text: The AI lead coordinates shared tools, evaluations, dependencies, and the release record. Its deployment authority must be delegated explicitly.
steps.evidence: Evaluation results, service commitments, dependency register, and documented delegated authority.

steps.label: Security & data
steps.title: Set and test the access boundary.
steps.text: Control owners specify permitted identities, data, and actions. A new repository or outbound tool triggers review of the changed scope.
steps.evidence: Role-based access tests, tool permissions, retained-data inventory, and exception decisions.

steps.label: Finance
steps.title: Make the investment case inspectable.
steps.text: Finance agrees cost allocation and challenges benefit assumptions. Time released is recorded separately from a demonstrated reduction in spend.
steps.evidence: Cost per accepted outcome, included and excluded expenses, benefit baseline, and review thresholds.

steps.label: Executive sponsor
steps.title: Resolve the tradeoff and record the decision.
steps.text: The sponsor decides portfolio priority and funding within applicable constraints. Approval records conditions, owners, and the next review, rather than treating release as permanent permission.
steps.evidence: A proceed, revise, or stop decision with conditions, delegated stop authority, and a review date.

questions: Who owns the business outcome and the acceptance criteria?
What authority does our AI lead actually hold?
Which changes trigger security, data, or specialist review?
Who can pause the workflow, and how is that decision escalated?
What evidence must finance and the sponsor see before further funding?

sources.title: McKinsey · How organizations are rewiring to capture value

research.label: Research background · AIR enterprise AI risk primer
research.note: Adapted from the organizational ownership themes in AIR’s August 16, 2026 primer. The mandate and Meridian scenario are Alphaworx’s proposed operating approach.

enterprise-ai-after-the-demo.quote: The next investment needs an operating case as well as a demonstration.
lab: Six questions before the next investment.
Explore Meridian’s proposed service assistant. Each topic pairs an operating response with a limitation and the evidence to request.

steps.label: Value
steps.title: What counts as completed, useful work?
steps.text: Response: define acceptance and compare the workflow with a baseline. Limit: reported time savings alone do not demonstrate a cash benefit.
steps.evidence: Accepted outputs, review effort, repeat work, and a documented benefit baseline.

steps.label: Data
steps.title: Which information can the assistant actually reach?
steps.text: Response: review source access and test retrieval by role. Limit: permission-aware retrieval still exposes content allowed by overly broad source permissions.
steps.evidence: Representative allow/deny tests and a record of connected sources.

steps.label: Actions
steps.title: What can it do after generating an answer?
steps.text: Response: restrict tools and enforce authorization downstream. Limit: a smaller action set does not guarantee correct answers or remove all failure modes.
steps.evidence: Permitted operations, approval conditions, and revocation tests.

steps.label: Reliability
steps.title: What happens when the normal path fails?
steps.text: Response: test difficult cases and provide escalation and fallback. Limit: a finite evaluation set cannot cover every future input or service change.
steps.evidence: Regression results, reviewed exceptions, and an exercised fallback.

steps.label: Providers
steps.title: Which changes depend on somebody else?
steps.text: Response: inventory dependencies and assign change monitoring. Limit: an alternative still requires evaluation and may have different capacity or contract terms.
steps.evidence: Dependency register, change owner, and migration rehearsal.

steps.label: Ownership
steps.title: Who can fund, approve, or stop this workflow?
steps.text: Response: agree delegated authority and review conditions. Limit: a named role only works when it has time, evidence, and the authority to act.
steps.evidence: Decision record, accountable owners, escalation route, and next review date.

questions: What evidence would make us expand, revise, or stop this workflow?
Have we priced accepted work including review and exceptions?
Can we demonstrate the data and action boundaries?
What is the remaining limitation after each proposed control?
Who owns the next decision and when will it be reviewed?
